miles-per-kwh-calculator.assumptionNote: Based on the energy you enter. Home charging adds about 8 to 15% charging loss, so the dashboard number and the wall-meter number differ slightly.
benefits: Compare EVs fairly: the same 4.0 mi/kWh benchmark works across every model.
Track battery health: a steady drop in efficiency can signal tire, brake, or battery issues.

faqs.a: Miles per kWh = miles driven divided by kWh used. It is the EV version of miles per gallon. Higher is better.
faqs.q: How do you calculate miles per kWh?

faqs.a: Most efficient EVs get 3.5 to 4.5 mi/kWh. Average drivers see 3.0 to 4.0. Below 2.5 usually means fast highway driving, heavy loads, cold weather, or a very large vehicle.
faqs.q: What is a good miles per kWh?

faqs.a: Wh per mile = 1000 / mi/kWh. So 4.0 mi/kWh equals 250 Wh/mi. Tesla and many EV dashboards show Wh/mi; this calculator shows both.
faqs.q: How do I convert mi/kWh to Wh per mile?

faqs.a: Multiply mi/kWh by 1.60934 to get km/kWh. This calculator shows that conversion automatically.
faqs.q: How do I convert to km per kWh?

faqs.a: Cold air is denser, tire pressure drops, cabin heating uses battery power, and batteries are less efficient when cold. Winter can cut efficiency by 20 to 40 percent.
faqs.q: Why does my EV lose efficiency in winter?

faqs.a: Roughly: MPGe = mi/kWh x 33.7. So 4.0 mi/kWh is about 135 MPGe. MPGe compares EVs to gasoline cars using the energy in a gallon of gas.
faqs.q: What is the difference between mi/kWh and MPGe?

miles-per-kwh-calculator.formula:
Miles per kWh = Miles driven / kWh used

Wh per mile = (kWh / Miles) x 1000 = 1000 / (mi/kWh)
km per kWh = mi/kWh x 1.60934
MPGe = mi/kWh x 33.7

Example: 300 miles / 75 kWh = 4.0 mi/kWh = 250 Wh/mi = 6.44 km/kWh.
howTo: Enter the kWh used for those miles (from your charger or the car's trip meter).
Read your miles per kWh, Wh per mile, and km per kWh.
Compare against the efficiency rating to see how your EV is doing.
keyFacts: Miles per kWh is the EV equivalent of miles per gallon. Higher is better.
Wh per mile is the same information flipped: 1000 / (mi/kWh).
Typical EVs: 3.0 to 4.5 mi/kWh. Hypermilers reach 5+; towing or fast highways drop under 2.5.
Speed is the biggest lever: aerodynamic drag grows with the square of speed.
Cold weather cuts efficiency 20 to 40% through heating, denser air, and battery chemistry.
Charging losses mean the wall meter reads 8 to 15% more than the battery received.
1 kWh = 3.6 megajoules. An efficient EV uses about 0.15 kWh per km.
Regenerative braking recovers energy in stop-and-go traffic, boosting city efficiency.
